steps.label: Cover's theorem
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp14 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 9 pages; this unit is self-study and is not taught in class; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Corner labelings
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP14, a self-study unit. Prerequisites: linear separability (KP03), lifting (KP13) and the binomial coefficient (the number of ways to pick i out of n). A dichotomy is one way of labeling N points with two classes; if a line can do it, it is a linear dichotomy. Three points in general position have 2 to the 3rd equal to 8 labelings and all are separable; the four corners of a square have 2 to the 4th equal to 16 labelings, and a program checks each one: 14 are separable. The 2 that fail pair the diagonal corners: top-left with bottom-right is XOR, and the same with the class names swapped is XNOR (computed by program). Next, the next page covers Cover's formula.

steps.label: Cover's formula
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the 16 labelings of the four corners. This page gives the counting formula. General position means that no l plus 1 of the points lie on one hyperplane of dimension l minus 1; in 2-D, no three points are collinear. Cover's formula: O(N, l) equals 2 times the sum over i from 0 to l of C(N minus 1, i). For N equal to 4 and l equal to 2: C(3, i) is 1, 3, 3, so O equals 2 times 7, that is 14. For N equal to 3: C(2, i) is 1, 2, 1 and O equals 2 times 4, that is 8, which is 2 to the 3rd. In general, when N is at most l plus 1, O equals 2 to the N and every labeling is separable. On the right is the table for l equal to 2 and N from 1 to 8: O is 2, 4, 8, 14, 22, 32, 44, 58 and 2 to the N is 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the separability probability.

steps.label: Separability probability
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on Cover's formula. This page turns the counts into probabilities. With random labels all 2 to the N labelings are equally likely, so the separability probability P equals O(N, l) over 2 to the N; when N is at most l plus 1, P equals 1. For l equal to 2 and N from 1 to 10, P is 1, 1, 1, 0.875, 0.6875, 0.5, 0.344, 0.227, 0.145, 0.090 (computed by program). As soon as N exceeds l plus 1, which is 3, the probability starts to fall, and at N equal to 6 it is exactly one half. Next, the next page covers the phase transition.

steps.label: Phase transition
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the separability probability. This page looks at the curves in higher dimensions. A phase transition is the turn where the probability drops from 1 to 0; the larger the dimension, the sharper the turn, like water freezing. Let N equal r times l plus 1, where r is the number of points over the degrees of freedom. At r equal to 2 the probability is exactly 1/2, in four steps: one, N equals 2l plus 2, so N minus 1 equals 2l plus 1; two, C(2l plus 1, i) equals C(2l plus 1, 2l plus 1 minus i), the front half mirrors the back half; three, the sum over i up to l is exactly half of the total, that is 2 to the 2l; four, O equals 2 times 2 to the 2l and P equals 1/2. The curves for l equal to 1, 3, 9, 19, 49, 99 all pass through (2, 1/2). P at r equal to 1.5 for l equal to 1, 19, 99 is 0.75, 0.97, 1.00; at r equal to 2.5 it is 0.31, 0.08, 0.0007 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the random trials.

steps.label: Random trials
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the phase transition. This page tests the formula with a random experiment. The setup is my own design and reproducible: each trial draws N standard-normal points in 2-D, gives each a random plus or minus 1 label, and a linear program checks whether a line separates the two classes; 1500 trials per N with seed 1. At N equal to 4 the measured value is 0.865 against 0.875 from the formula, a gap of 0.010; at N equal to 6 it is 0.503 against 0.500, a gap of 0.003. The standard error of 1500 trials is about the square root of 0.25 over 1500, which is 0.013, so both gaps are within about one standard error and formula and measurement agree (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the effect of lifting.

steps.label: Effect of lifting
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the random trials. This page shows the effect of lifting. With the same kind of random points and labels, N equal to 6 and 1500 trials: with the original x1 and x2, l equals 2, the formula predicts 0.5 and the measurement is 0.494; adding the three quadratic coordinates x1 squared, x2 squared and x1 times x2 gives l equal to 5, and N equal to 6 does not exceed l plus 1 equal to 6, so P equals 1 and all 1500 trials are separable, 1.000 (computed by program). The only difference is the three added quadratic coordinates. Next, the next page covers how many dimensions are enough.

steps.label: How many dimensions
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the effect of lifting. This page fixes N at 100 and varies the dimension l. Once N exceeds l plus 1 some labelings fail; when N exceeds 2 times l plus 1 the separability probability is below one half. In the table, l equal to 40, 48, 49, 56, 60, 68 gives P equal to 0.035, 0.42, 0.5, 0.92, 0.987, 0.9999 (computed by program). To separate random labels by lifting, the dimension must reach about half the data size or more. Next, the next page covers separable is not generalizable.

steps.label: Not generalization
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on how many dimensions are enough. This page handles a common myth: if lifting separates the training data, new data will be classified correctly too. The setup is my own design and reproducible: 5 standard-normal points in 2-D with random plus or minus 1 labels, a separating hyperplane found by linear programming in the quadratic features, that is 5 dimensions, 300 times with seed 1; each time 200 new points, also randomly labeled, are predicted by that hyperplane. Result: all 300 runs found one, since N equal to 5 does not exceed l plus 1 equal to 6, as the formula says, and training is all correct; new points are right only 50.4% of the time on average, which is guessing (computed by program). Lifting only guarantees that the training data separate; only data with structure teach anything, and generalization has to be examined separately. Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on separable is not generalizable. Two exercises with N equal to 5 points in general position. Q1: O(5, 2) and P for l equal to 2. C(4, i) is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, so O equals 2 times 1 plus 4 plus 6, which is 22, and P equals 22 over 32, which is 0.6875; check: 22 matches the table on page 2. Q2: raise l to 3, then O(5, 3) equals 2 times 1 plus 4 plus 6 plus 4, which is 30, and P equals 30 over 32, which is 0.9375; one more dimension lifts the separability probability from 0.6875 to 0.9375 (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
